extracted.intended_audience: intellectual property attorneys—patent prosecutors, litigators, and counseling/opinion counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Practitioner-focused guidance on liability for induced and divided patent infringement (particularly for method claims), and recommended claim-drafting, contract, litigation, and opinion strategies in light of Akamai and McKesson. Emphasizes what must be proved for inducement and how to draft and litigate to avoid or leverage divided-infringement risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement requirement (single-entity rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct patent infringement requires that a single party make, use, sell, offer to sell, or import a device that contains all the limitations of a patent claim, or perform a method that contains all the limitations of a patent claim; intent is irrelevant and the statute creates strict liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single-entity rule can be satisfied by a party acting personally or vicariously (direction or control/agency). To establish direction or control, every step must be attributable to the controlling party; merely providing instructions or cooperating at arm's length is insufficient. Contracts must obligate the third party to perform the claimed method steps to show direction or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate direct infringement for indirect liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement (induced or contributory) still requires that infringement actually occur—i.e., indirect liability cannot attach without an underlying direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically this meant a single-party direct infringement, but Akamai modifies the application in the inducement context (see separate entries). Unsuccessful attempts to induce or contribute do not create liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement general elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, when a single actor actively and knowingly aids and abets another actor to infringe a patent, the first actor is liable for induced infringement: (1) the inducer causes, urges, encourages, or aids in the infringing conduct; and (2) the induced conduct is ultimately carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inducement requires proof of both the induced acts and that those acts were performed. The inducement provisions listed in the Federal Circuit include advising, encouraging, urging, causing, and aiding. Proof must show the acts were in fact performed by the induced parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific intent requirement for inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific intent requirement for inducement requires more than an intent to cause the acts that produce direct infringement—the inducer must know that the induced acts constitute patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability may also exist where the defendant acted with willful blindness (subjectively believed high probability a patent existed and took deliberate actions to avoid learning that fact). Thus evidence of actual knowledge of the patent or willful blindness is critical to proving inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful blindness doctrine as substitute for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful blindness applies where the defendant subjectively believed there was a high probability that a patent existed and deliberately avoided learning that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents defendants from insulating themselves from liability by deliberate ignorance. Look for evidence of conscious steps taken to avoid patent-related facts when assessing inducement intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement elements and territorial limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement applies when an entity offers to sell or sells a component or material for use in practicing a patented process that is a material part of the invention, knowing it is especially made or adapted for infringement and not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributory infringement has a territorial limitation requiring the contributory acts to occur in the United States. Knowledge that the component was especially made/adapted for infringement is required; general sales of staple goods for substantial noninfringing use will not support contributory liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Akamai/McKesson holding on inducement liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit (en banc) held that liability for induced infringement under §271(b) may be found even if the steps of a patented method are divided among multiple parties — it is not necessary to prove that all steps were committed by a single entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court focused on §271(b)’s text and policy, distinguishing it from §271(a). This means inducement liability can be asserted when an actor causes or induces others to collectively perform the claimed steps, so long as the elements of inducement (including knowledge/willful blindness) and performance of steps are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elements for inducement under Akamai (Limelight fact pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per the Federal Circuit’s guidance in Akamai, Limelight can be liable for inducing infringement if it can be shown that: (1) Limelight knew of Akamai’s patent; (2) Limelight performed all but one of the method steps; (3) Limelight induced the content providers to perform the final step; and (4) the content providers in fact performed that final step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete checklist that district courts were instructed to apply on remand for similar divided-performance inducement theories. Gathering evidence on each element (knowledge, which steps performed, communications/encouragement, and proof that third parties performed the remaining steps) is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elements for inducement under Akamai (McKesson fact pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per the Federal Circuit’s guidance in McKesson, Epic can be liable for inducing infringement if it can be shown that: (1) Epic knew of McKesson’s patent; (2) Epic induced the performance of the steps of the method claimed; and (3) those steps were in fact performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McKesson reflects a scenario where the defendant induced multiple third parties to collectively perform the method but itself did not perform any steps. Emphasizes the centrality of knowledge and proof that induced acts took place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overruling of BMC Resources (scope limited to inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit overruled its 2007 BMC Resources panel decision to the extent BMC had required that induced infringement be predicated on a single entity being liable for direct infringement; however, the majority declined to disturb the law of divided infringement as applied to direct infringement under §271(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should understand that the single-entity rule remains for direct infringement analysis, but BMC’s limitation is lifted in the inducement context per Akamai — creating asymmetry between §§271(a) and (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft core claims targeted to a single party
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecutors should, where possible, focus on core claims targeted toward a single party (single-entity method claims) to avoid divided-infringement issues and to preserve the ability to sue for direct infringement under §271(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-entity method claims are preferred because direct infringement is strict liability and the law and damages rules for direct infringement are better settled. This also hedges against possible Supreme Court reversal of Akamai/McKesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer system/product claims where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where technology permits, draft system or apparatus claims instead of method claims because recent cases treat system claims differently and a party may infringe a claimed system by merely using the system and obtaining benefit from it (ability to place the system as a whole into service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System claims can avoid divided-infringement problems because infringement may be found without physical control/possession of every element. Assess whether system claim forms better capture the commercial actor you expect to target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft method claims to prevent steps from occurring outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecutors should draft method claims to prevent steps from occurring outside the United States since a method claim is infringed only if all steps are performed inside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, include claim language that requires acts to occur in the United States or recite steps in a manner that makes non-U.S. performance less likely; this can limit divided-infringement exposure and avoid territorial gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate or rephrase steps performed by separate actors (claim drafting technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a second entity performs certain steps, consider eliminating those steps from the claim or drafting around them (for example, claim 'transmitting the data to a receiver' and omit a recitation of 'receiving the data').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, draft multiple independent claims directed separately to each potential actor (one claim for the end user, another for the provider), to preserve direct-infringement options and avoid reliance on inducement theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement single-entity claims with multi-party claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement single-entity method claims with claims directed to multiple parties where appropriate, to provide additional protection under potential inducement theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layered claim sets—core single-actor claims for direct infringement, plus claims that capture multi-actor or induced-performance scenarios—to maximize enforceability across business models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims to capture actions of several unconnected actors (when useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting method claims to incorporate the actions of several unconnected actors may satisfy inducement standards and help capture practices involving distributed responsibilities (e.g., diagnostics, cloud services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims can facilitate enforcement under inducement after Akamai, but require careful attention to proving knowledge and actual performance of steps by the multiple actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract drafting to avoid direction or control exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: In contracting, avoid language or obligations that suggest an agency relationship or impose duties that could be used to show direction or control; maintain arm’s-length relationships to minimize risk of being attributed direct-infringement liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs and defendants should investigate contractual relationships. Indemnifiers should consider carving out an exception for inducement liability in indemnity provisions as part of risk allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation defense strategy—show absence of direction or control
rubrics_metrics.description: Accused infringers should consider demonstrating the absence of direction or control where multiple entities are implicated, because joint (direct) infringement remains a defense and could obviate the need to address inducement intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show evidence of independent decisionmaking, lack of contractual obligation, lack of agency, and arm’s-length dealings to rebut vicarious-liability theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on patentee to prove inducement elements (including intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees pursuing inducement theories must prove both that the inducer displayed the requisite level of intent (knowledge or willful blindness) and that all steps of the claimed method were performed (even if by multiple actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because inducement requires a mental state, fact issues about knowledge/willful blindness are likely to be disputed—gather direct evidence of knowledge, communications encouraging actions, marketing materials, or circumstantial evidence of deliberate avoidance of patent-related information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction strategy shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction may be used strategically: patentees may seek constructions that attribute method steps to a single actor, while accused infringers may argue constructions that attribute steps to different actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of claim construction can materially affect whether direct infringement is found; tailor claim construction arguments to support either direct-infringement or divided-infringement defenses as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom-to-operate and opinion practice implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom-to-operate (FTO) analyses and non-infringement opinions that were based on absence of a single infringing entity may need reconsideration post-Akamai; practitioners should more thoroughly investigate how steps are performed and by whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an opinion depended on the lack of a single entity performing all steps, re-evaluate in light of inducement/liability for multiple-actor scenarios and consider whether additional factual inquiry or claim amendments are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and remedial uncertainty for multi-actor inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unclear how damages should be calculated for induced infringement where multiple parties complete the patented method steps; allocation/apportionment questions and jurisdictional limitations on suing underlying actors remain open questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate contested expert analyses and novel apportionment arguments; consider the risk that some underlying actors may be beyond the court’s jurisdiction and strategize relief requests accordingly (injunctions against inducers, damages allocation theories, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limited to inducement of method claims; open questions remain
rubrics_metrics.description: The Akamai and McKesson decisions are limited to inducement theories for method claims; the court expressly declined to resolve whether direct infringement can be found where no single entity performs all claimed steps under §271(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not assume the law of divided infringement for direct infringement has changed—many aspects remain unsettled and may be reviewed by the Supreme Court or addressed legislatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogous criminal and tort principles to support inducement liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit relied on analogies to criminal aiding-and-abetting and joint tortfeasance principles to justify allowing inducement liability even when intermediate actors are innocent or not liable as direct infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analogies provide persuasive context when arguing for inducement liability—showing that law in other fields treats the inducer as a principal even if intermediaries are innocent.
